translation: The limitless sea noise didn't cease for a minute.
It rolled in long waves, sometimes intensifying, sometimes dying down.
And the wind would start to rustle in the bare trees and then fall silent, just like me listening to the flow of the night.
But it wasn't gone I knew it was here by the smell of wet pebbles and barely perceptible trembling of a single plane tree leaf.
I had noticed this stubborn grey leaf during daylight but now at night, it seemed like a little living creature my solitary wakeful friend.
Occasionally from afar, from town direction gunshots reached out echoing back through barking dogs after each shot fired.
Then far out at sea a faint light blinked on and off momentarily.
He made me look at these things more closely and for longer than we usually do, and I began to see in them many qualities that had previously gone unnoticed.
For example, the snub-nosed yellow stone contained many tiny seashells firmly embedded within it;
a few flowers still clung to the broom bushes, perched atop sturdy stems like sodden, wrinkled golden butterflies patiently awaiting the sun.
Yet the sun rarely broke through the fog as a blurred white splodge, offering neither warmth nor shadow.
Underneath the solitary old plane tree with lemon spots on its trunk lay leaves that seemed cut out of dull green velvet.
A stream of ants ran along an iron gate carrying their last supplies for the winter into underground bunkers while beneath an anchor chain lived a little timid frog.
During the night on the other side of the river, someone began to wave a lantern and shout elongated calls.
My Uncle Ilko and I went out onto the bank.
The river was roaring.
Water rushed over the dam in a cold waterfall.
The late night was dense, not a single star overhead.
A wild freshness from the overflowing river-bed and thawing earth blew in our faces.
Yet all that while, someone kept waving a lantern on that shore and shouting; however, over the noise of roaring river one could not make out any words.
When the coffin was carried out to the porch, I saw on the other side of the river an old carriage, horses unharnessed and tethered to it, and a small woman in black my mom.
She stood motionless on the bank.
From there, she saw how they were carrying out my father.
Then she fell to her knees and collapsed with her face onto the sand.
No, replied the grandfather.
It's true, they didn't see each other again.
Ostap began to lose his eyesight.
He then decided to go all the way to Petersburg, wanting to see that woman before he was entirely blind.
He got as far as the Tsar's capital and learned that she had died; perhaps she could not withstand their separation.
Ostap found her tombstone of white marble in a cemetery, glanced at it, and his heart broke over the iron rose lying on her stone.
That woman had bequeathed him to place a rose on her grave forever.
And so Ostap began his lamentation and perhaps he died en route or in a market under a wagonload even before he became completely blind Amen!
On the other side, Countess Branicka's reserved forest rose up the slope.
The sun could not break through the powerful greenery of this forest.
Only occasionally would a solitary ray cut diagonally across the thicket and reveal to us the astounding power of vegetation.
Like sparkling specks, small birds would swoop into this ray.
They squeaked as they chased each other and dived into foliage, as if into green water.
I filled a bucket with water from the pond, tossed some grass into the water, and waited.
The red floats stood motionless in the water.
Then one of them began to shudder, making faint circles before it suddenly dived or quickly swam off to the side.
My father jerked it up, the line tightened and the walnut rod bent into a bow as there began a splashing and commotion above the foggy pond.
The water rippled, shaking up lily pads as beetles hurriedly scurried off in all directions only for a flailing golden shimmer to appear from deep within its mysterious depths.

You wouldn't be able to tell what was happening until my father hauled out onto some flattened grass a heavy crucian carp laying on its side, panting and flicking its fins with an astonishing scent of underwater dominion wafting from its scales.
Yasha timed himself.
We knew it was a seven-minute walk from Sturdza Alley to Landesman's sanatorium.
There we always felt utterly safe behind the high fence and iron gates, especially if we didn't light any incense burners.
Nearing a side entrance, Yasha tripped.
In later recollections of what happened in Sturdza Alley, he maintained that whenever you want to do something very well, you'll inevitably mess up because of some triviality.
As for me, I quietly blamed his unbearable stride for everything that happened.
But I kept quiet so as not to upset Yasha.
We sneaked down the alley.
I suggested that we should walk on the side with the archway, stop just before it and listen carefully, then rush past it quickly and silently.
My plan was mathematically precise, in my opinion.
If there were people in the archway, they might not notice us at all whilst if we walked on the opposite side from it, they could spot us from afar.

I calculated that in the latter case we would expose ourselves to the dangerous archway or rather be visible to anyone who might be hiding there five times longer, therefore increasing our chance of being noticed by five-fold.
I would wake up in the morning to the hot sun striking the white walls.
Red and yellow hollyhocks swayed behind the open window.
A nasturtium bloom peaked into the room, housing a furry bee.
Frozen, I watched as it backed out irritably from the tight flower.
Endless light streams, gentle waves of river reflection, ran across the ceiling.
The river was murmuring just near-by.
